text: Europe and Africa are only thirteen to fourteen kilometres apart. That is shorter than the sea section of India's longest sea bridge, Atal Setu in Mumbai, which runs about sixteen and a half kilometres over water. Yet there is no bridge, no tunnel and no road between the two continents. So why has nobody built one? And why, in twenty twenty six, are Spain and Morocco still paying millions for studies?
This is the true scale of the gap between two continents.

The gap is the Strait of Gibraltar. To the west is the Atlantic Ocean, to the east the Mediterranean Sea. To the north is Spain, to the south is Morocco. The strait is about fifty eight kilometres long. At its western end it is about forty three kilometres wide, but at the narrowest point, between Point Marroquí in Spain and Point Cires in Morocco, it shrinks to about thirteen or fourteen kilometres, depending on how you measure it. Ferries already cross the strait every day, in as little as thirty five minutes.

And it is one of the busiest stretches of water on Earth. More than one hundred thousand vessels pass through the strait every year, because it is the Mediterranean's only natural opening to the open ocean. Whatever you build here, the ships still have to get through. So the first question is simple: how deep is the water?

Problem number one is depth. Where the strait is narrowest, the seabed drops to around nine hundred metres. Further west, there is an underwater ridge called the Camarinal Sill, where the water is only about two hundred and eighty to three hundred metres deep. That is the shallowest route across, but it makes the crossing much longer. For comparison, the Channel Tunnel between Britain and France reaches about one hundred and fifteen metres below sea level. Japan's Seikan Tunnel, one of the deepest railway tunnels ever built, runs about two hundred and forty metres below the sea.

So what about a bridge? The engineer T. Y. Lin once proposed one across the narrows: about fourteen kilometres long, with towers about nine hundred and ten metres tall and a main span of five thousand metres. Today the longest suspension span in the world is the nineteen fifteen Çanakkale Bridge in Turkey, at two thousand and twenty three metres, with towers of three hundred and thirty four metres. Lin's bridge would need a span about two and a half times the world record, and towers almost three times as tall.

Then there is the water itself. The strait has two currents stacked on top of each other. Fresher Atlantic water flows east into the Mediterranean on the surface. Underneath, heavier, saltier Mediterranean water flows west, out into the Atlantic. This happens because the Mediterranean loses more water to evaporation than its rivers and rain put back. Any pillar or tunnel has to live with that never-ending exchange.

Problem number two is the ground. The strait sits where two tectonic plates meet. The African Plate is slowly moving north against the Eurasian Plate, and the Azores Gibraltar fault zone runs through the region, which has seen severe earthquakes. That is why, in December twenty twenty five, Spain and Morocco agreed a three year joint study of earthquakes, tsunamis and the movement of the seabed.

And the seabed is not solid granite. It is mostly clay rich flysch covered by younger sediments. Engineers are most worried about two deep ancient channels filled with clay. A tunnel boring machine would have to pass through them. Herrenknecht, the German company that builds tunnel boring machines, studied the project and reported in June twenty twenty five that it is technically possible with today's technology, but extremely complex.

The depth of the strait itself tells an incredible story. About six million years ago, the link to the Atlantic closed. The Mediterranean was cut off, and most of it evaporated, leaving a salty basin far below sea level. Then, about five point three three million years ago, the Atlantic broke back in. Scientists think about ninety percent of the sea refilled in somewhere between a few months and two years, with water pouring through at about three times the flow of the Amazon River. That flood helped carve the strait as deep as it is today.

People have dreamed of crossing it for a long time. Spain proposed a tunnel as early as nineteen thirty. In nineteen seventy nine, the kings of Spain and Morocco signed a joint declaration to study a fixed link. Spain set up a company called SECEGSA in nineteen eighty one, and Morocco has its own partner, SNED. Studies came and went for decades. Then, in twenty twenty three, the two countries relaunched the plan.

Here is what is on the table now. Not a bridge, and not a road. It is a railway tunnel, with no cars. The route under study crosses from Punta Paloma in Spain to Punta Malabata, near Tangier. The full rail link is about sixty five kilometres, with roughly twenty eight kilometres under the sea. It would be two single track tubes with a service tunnel between them, and cross passages every three hundred and forty metres. To pass under the Camarinal Sill, the deepest point would be about four hundred and seventy five metres below sea level.

Put that next to the record holders. The Channel Tunnel is about fifty kilometres long, with thirty eight kilometres under the sea. The Seikan Tunnel is about fifty four kilometres long, with twenty three kilometres under the sea. The Gibraltar link would be longer than both, and roughly twice as deep below sea level as Seikan. It would be one of the deepest railway tunnels ever attempted.

So, where is it now? Spain's own section alone is estimated at more than eight and a half billion euros, and estimates for the whole project range from fifteen to thirty billion. In March twenty twenty six, Spain approved another one point seven three million euros for technical studies. In November, reports said Morocco set aside about eleven million euros for more studies in twenty twenty seven. The next big step is a test tunnel, called an exploratory gallery, to check the rock. A decision on that is expected around twenty twenty seven, and building it could take six to nine years.

That means it will not be ready for the twenty thirty football World Cup, which Spain and Morocco are co-hosting. Most estimates now say twenty thirty five to twenty forty at the earliest, and no final decision to build has been taken. Politics matters too: this would be a direct rail link between the European Union's outer border and North Africa, and after border tensions this year, some voices in Spain are questioning the whole idea.

If it does happen, the payoff is huge. A train could cross between the two continents in about thirty minutes, linking Spain's high speed network to Morocco's Al Boraq, Africa's first high speed railway. For the first time, you could ride a train from Europe into Africa.

So, why is there no bridge between Europe and Africa? Deep water, a busy shipping lane, two currents, moving plates and buried clay channels, all in a gap of only about fourteen kilometres. Would you take a thirty minute train under the sea between two continents, or stick with the ferry? Tell me in the comments. And subscribe to True Scale for the world at its real size.
